questions.from: Four modules back — What Code Actually Is
questions.prompt: From What Code Actually Is: what makes an instruction something a computer can actually act on?

options.label: It's phrased politely
It's exact enough that nothing is left for judgment
It's written in a well-known language

questions.explanation: Exactness is the whole requirement — a checkable rule with no gap left for judgment, regardless of language or tone.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: Loops: the same work over many items
description: A loop runs the same block of code repeatedly instead of it being copy-pasted by hand — the single biggest lever for programs that do real, repetitive work.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what a loop does that copy-pasted code doesn't
Read a basic for loop and count how many times its body runs
Read a basic for...of loop over a list of values

contentSections.body: You need to print a reminder for three medications, one line each. Copy-pasting `console.log` three times works today. It stops working the moment there's a fourth medication, or the wording needs to change — now you're hunting down every copy by hand.

contentSections.question: Both print the same three lines. What's the actual difference that matters?

options.label: Nothing — they're functionally identical in every way that matters
The looped version says "do this 3 times" in one place, instead of three separate places
The copy-pasted version runs faster

feedback.same: They print identical output right now, but that's not the whole comparison — think about what happens the moment the number of reminders or the wording needs to change.
feedback.one_place: Right. The loop states the repeated instruction exactly once. Changing the wording, or changing how many times it runs, means editing one line instead of finding and fixing every copy.
feedback.faster: At this small scale the speed difference is irrelevant either way — the real difference is about maintenance, not execution speed.

contentSections.concept: A loop is a block of code that runs repeatedly, instead of being written out by hand once per repetition. It exists for exactly the same reason functions will later in this phase: to say a thing once instead of copy-pasting it, so there's exactly one place to fix or change it.

contentSections.body: A loop says a repeated instruction once. Copy-pasting says it once per copy — and every copy has to be found and fixed separately.

contentSections.title: Looping over a list of real values

contentSections.body: Counting to 3 is one kind of repetition. Going through an actual list — three real medication names, not just the numbers 0 through 2 — is the far more common real case, and JavaScript has a loop shape built specifically for it.

contentSections.hint: for...of goes through a list value by value — name takes each real item from meds in turn, not a counting number.
contentSections.answer: Take: Ibuprofen, then Take: Omeprazole, then Take: Vitamin D — one line per item in the list, in order. Unlike the counting for loop from pod 1, `for...of` hands you the actual value from the list each time (here, each medication name) rather than a number you'd have to use to look the value up.

contentSections.body: `["Ibuprofen", "Omeprazole", "Vitamin D"]` is a list of values — square brackets, comma-separated. This track covers lists properly soon; for now, just recognize the shape and its matching loop: `for (const name of meds) { ... }` runs its body once per item in `meds`, with `name` holding the actual current item each time — no counting, no index math, just "for each one of these, do this." It's the natural loop to reach for whenever you already have a collection of real values rather than a fixed number of repetitions.
for...of hands you each real item from a list directly — no counting required.

title: Looping a known number of times
description: The for loop's three parts — where the counter starts, when it stops, and how it changes — decide exactly how many times the body runs, and getting one of the three slightly wrong is the single most common loop bug there is.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the three parts of a for loop and what each controls
Predict exactly how many times a for loop's body runs for given start/condition/step values
Write a for loop that runs a specific, stated number of times

contentSections.body: `for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++)` looks like one dense line, but it's really three completely separate instructions stacked together — mixing up which one controls what is exactly where off-by-one mistakes come from.

contentSections.question: Put these in the order they actually correspond to the three parts of `for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++)`, left to right.
steps: let i = 0 — set the counter's starting value, once, before the loop begins
i < 5 — checked before every single pass; the loop stops the moment this is false
i++ — runs after each pass, moving the counter toward the stopping condition
contentSections.explanation: The three parts run in a specific rhythm: the start happens exactly once, then check-run-step repeats: check the condition, if true run the body, then step the counter, then check again. The loop ends the first time the condition check comes back false — which is always checked before a pass, never after.

contentSections.body: Each part has exactly one job. `let i = 0` runs once, before anything else, setting where counting begins. `i < 5` is checked before every pass — including the very first — and the loop stops the instant it's false. `i++` runs after each pass's body finishes, moving the counter closer to the stopping point. A bug in any one of the three changes the loop's behavior in a different way: wrong start shifts every printed number, wrong condition changes how many passes happen, wrong step could skip values or never reach the stopping condition at all.
Start, condition, step — three separate jobs. A bug in any one changes the loop differently from a bug in another.
"Run this 5 times" sounds simple, and yet a huge share of a beginner's early loop bugs are the printed count being off by exactly one — one extra pass, or one missing.

contentSections.question: How many times does the loop body run, and what does count end up being?
contentSections.explanation: 6, not 5. `i` takes the values 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 — `<=` includes 5 itself, which adds one extra pass beyond what `<` would give. This is the classic off-by-one: swapping `<` for `<=` (or the reverse) changes the total count by exactly one, and it's an easy swap to make without noticing, especially when copying a loop from another context with a slightly different intent.

contentSections.body: The fix for off-by-one bugs isn't a trick — it's tracing the actual values the counter takes, the way the exercise above just did, instead of trusting a quick glance. A reliable habit: for `i < n` starting at 0, the loop runs exactly `n` times, with `i` taking values `0` through `n - 1`. For `i <= n` starting at 0, it runs `n + 1` times, with `i` taking values `0` through `n`. Whichever one matches the count you actually want is the one to use — and it's worth deliberately checking, every time, rather than assuming.
For i < n starting at 0: exactly n passes. For i <= n starting at 0: n + 1 passes. Trace the actual values, don't guess.

title: Looping until something is true, and the one that never ends
description: A while loop repeats for as long as a condition holds, with no built-in counter — which makes it exactly the right tool for "keep going until," and exactly the wrong tool to write carelessly, since nothing stops it from running forever if that condition never changes.

learningObjectives.text: Read a while loop and predict how many passes it runs for a stated starting value
Explain what causes a while loop to run forever
Identify the missing update that would turn an infinite loop into a working one

contentSections.title: Repeat while a condition holds — no counting required

contentSections.body: "Keep spending spoons until you run out" isn't a fixed number of repetitions the way a for loop expects — it depends entirely on the actual value, which is exactly the situation a while loop is built for.

contentSections.question: What decides when this loop stops?

options.label: A fixed number of repetitions, set at the top like a for loop
Whenever the condition spoonsLeft > 0 becomes false
After exactly 3 lines of code inside the body run

feedback.fixed: There's no counter set up front the way `for (let i = 0; i < 3; ...)` has one — a while loop has no built-in idea of how many times it'll run.
feedback.condition: Right. `while (spoonsLeft > 0)` is checked before every pass, and the loop keeps going for as long as that check is true — it stops the instant it isn't, however many passes that takes.
feedback.linecount: The number of lines inside the body has nothing to do with how many times the whole loop repeats — the body itself runs multiple times, as a unit, each pass.

contentSections.concept: A while loop repeats for as long as its condition is true, with no built-in sense of a fixed count. It's the right tool exactly when you don't know in advance how many times something needs to happen — only the condition under which it should keep happening.

contentSections.body: A while loop repeats until its condition is false — and nothing makes that condition false except code you write inside the body.

Delete one line from a working while loop — the one that actually updates the value being checked — and the program doesn't crash. It just runs forever, printing the same thing over and over until something outside the program forces it to stop.

contentSections.question: What's actually wrong?

options.label: spoonsLeft was set to the wrong starting value
Nothing inside the loop body ever changes spoonsLeft, so the condition never becomes false
console.log doesn't work correctly inside while loops

feedback.start: 3 is a perfectly reasonable starting value — the problem isn't where spoonsLeft begins, it's that it never moves from there.
feedback.noupdate: Right. `spoonsLeft > 0` is checked before every pass, and since nothing inside the body ever changes `spoonsLeft`, that check is true forever — the loop has no way to reach a stopping point.
feedback.logbug: console.log works completely normally here — it's printing exactly what it's told to, exactly as many times as the loop body runs, which unfortunately is infinitely.

contentSections.mechanism: An infinite loop happens when a while loop's condition depends on a value that never actually changes inside the body. The fix is always the same shape: identify what the condition is checking, and make sure something inside the loop genuinely moves that value toward making the condition false eventually — here, restoring `spoonsLeft = spoonsLeft - 1;` inside the body.

contentSections.body: Every while loop needs an honest answer to "what, specifically, changes on each pass to eventually make this condition false?" If the answer is "nothing" — the condition checks a value that's never touched inside the body — that's an infinite loop waiting to happen, whether or not it's obvious on first read. This is worth checking deliberately every time you write a while loop, not just when one already got stuck.
Before trusting a while loop, ask: what inside the body actually changes the value the condition depends on?

title: Breaking out early and skipping an item
description: break exits a loop immediately, for good. continue skips just the current pass and moves on. They look similar and do genuinely different things — mixing them up quietly changes what the rest of the loop does.

learningObjectives.text: Predict the output of a loop containing break
Predict the output of a loop containing continue
Explain the difference between break and continue in one sentence each

contentSections.title: break: stop the whole loop, right now

contentSections.body: You're searching a medication list for one specific name. Once it's found, there's no reason to keep checking the rest of the list — `break` is exactly the instruction for "stop looking, we're done."

contentSections.question: This is meant to stop checking the list the moment Omeprazole is found, but it still checks Vitamin D too. What's missing?

options.label: found should start as true, not false
A break statement right after found = true
The if condition is comparing the wrong thing

feedback.start: found starting as false is correct — it genuinely hasn't been found yet when the loop begins. That's not the missing piece.
feedback.break: Right. Setting found to true records that it was found, but nothing tells the loop to actually stop — that's exactly what break does, and it's missing here.
feedback.condition: name === "Omeprazole" correctly identifies the match — the comparison itself isn't the problem.

contentSections.flawExplanation: Without `break`, the loop has no reason to stop early — it keeps running through every remaining item even after the thing it was looking for has already been found. Adding `break;` right after `found = true;` makes the loop exit immediately on the matching pass, so Vitamin D is never checked at all.

contentSections.body: `break` immediately exits the loop it's inside — no more passes, nothing after it in the loop runs, execution jumps straight to whatever comes after the loop entirely. It's the right tool exactly when continuing to loop after some condition is met would just be wasted work: found what you were searching for, hit a value that means the rest genuinely doesn't matter, satisfied whatever the loop existed to check.
break exits the whole loop immediately — nothing after it, in this pass or any later one, runs.

contentSections.title: continue: skip this one, keep the loop going

contentSections.body: A dose list has one bad entry — a negative number that shouldn't have gotten in. You don't want to stop processing the whole list over one bad value; you want to skip just that one and keep going.

contentSections.question: Which of these correctly describe what continue does here?

items.label: It skips console.log for the current pass only, when dose is -1
The loop still checks 8 and 400 after skipping -1
It stops the entire loop the moment a negative dose is found
It removes -1 from the doses list

explanation.skip_one: Correct — continue jumps to the next pass immediately, so console.log never runs for the pass where dose is -1.
explanation.loop_keeps_going: Correct — this is the core difference from break. The loop carries on normally to 8 and 400 after skipping just the one bad value.
explanation.stops_loop: This describes break, not continue. continue explicitly does the opposite — it keeps the loop running, just skips the current item.
explanation.removes_item: continue has no effect on the list itself — doses still contains -1 afterward, it's just that this one pass through the loop didn't act on it.

contentSections.synthesis: continue and break both interrupt a loop, but in genuinely different ways — continue skips one pass and carries on; break ends the loop for good. Reading which one a piece of code uses tells you a lot about what it's actually meant to do.

contentSections.body: The distinction in one line each: **break** means "stop the whole loop, right now." **continue** means "skip the rest of this one pass, but keep looping." Confusing them is a genuinely easy mistake — both interrupt normal flow, both are typed as a single word — but they produce very different results: reaching for `break` when you meant `continue` throws away every item after the current one; reaching for `continue` when you meant `break` keeps needlessly checking items you already know you don't need.
break stops the loop for good. continue skips just this pass and keeps going. Confusing them changes what the rest of the loop does.

title: Building something up as you loop
description: The accumulator pattern — a variable started before the loop, updated on every pass — is how a loop produces one real result (a total, a count, a combined message) instead of just repeating an action.

learningObjectives.text: Write an accumulator variable that sums values across a loop
Trace an accumulator's value across each pass of a loop
Diagnose an accumulator that was declared inside the loop by mistake

contentSections.title: A running total, one pass at a time

contentSections.body: A loop that only prints things doesn't leave anything behind once it's done. Adding up a list of medication doses needs the loop to actually produce a number you can use afterward — that's what an accumulator is for.

contentSections.question: What is `total` actually doing across the three passes of this loop?

options.label: Getting overwritten with just the current dose each time
Accumulating — each pass adds to whatever it already held
Staying at 0 the whole time, and only changing at the very end

feedback.overwrite: That would be `total = dose;` — but the actual line is `total = total + dose;`, which explicitly keeps the old value and adds to it, rather than replacing it.
feedback.accumulate: Right. `total = total + dose` reads whatever total currently holds, adds the current dose, and reassigns — so each pass builds on the result of the last one instead of starting over.
feedback.stays_zero: total changes on every single pass, not just at the end — by the time the loop finishes, it's been reassigned three separate times.

contentSections.concept: An **accumulator** is a variable created before a loop starts (here, `let total = 0;`) that gets updated — not replaced with something unrelated, but built on — during every pass. It's how a loop turns "do this repeatedly" into "produce one combined result," whether that's a sum, a count, or a combined piece of text.

contentSections.body: The shape is always the same: initialize the accumulator **before** the loop (`let total = 0;`), then update it **inside** the loop body using its own current value (`total = total + dose;`). The starting value matters and depends on what's being built: `0` for a sum, `0` for a count, `""` (empty string) for text being assembled piece by piece. Getting the starting value wrong — starting a sum at 1 instead of 0, say — throws off every single result that follows from it.
An accumulator starts before the loop and updates using its own current value on every pass — that's what turns repetition into one real result.

contentSections.title: The accumulator that resets itself every pass

contentSections.body: One character of placement — whether a variable's declaration sits inside or outside the loop's curly braces — is the entire difference between a working running total and one that quietly only ever remembers the last item.

contentSections.question: What's actually wrong?

options.label: total = total + dose is the wrong formula
let total = 0 is inside the loop body, so it resets to 0 every single pass
doses should be a while loop instead of for...of

feedback.formula: total = total + dose is exactly the right formula for accumulating — that line isn't the problem here.
feedback.scope: Right. Because `let total = 0;` is inside the loop's braces, it runs fresh on every pass — total gets reset to 0, then has just the current dose added, then the next pass resets it again. There's never a chance for it to genuinely accumulate across passes.
feedback.looptype: for...of is a completely appropriate loop for going through a list of doses — switching loop types wouldn't fix where the declaration sits.

contentSections.mechanism: An accumulator has to be declared exactly once, outside the loop, so its value persists and builds across every pass. Declaring it inside the loop body means it's recreated fresh on every single pass — whatever it accumulated on the previous pass is gone the instant the next one starts, because a brand-new variable with the same name, starting at 0 again, has just been created.

contentSections.body: This is a genuinely common and genuinely quiet bug, because the code still runs — it just produces a wrong number instead of an error, exactly the kind of failure Module 1's type lessons warned about with silent coercion. The fix is always the same: check that anything meant to persist across passes of a loop is declared once, before the loop's opening brace, not inside it.
Declare an accumulator once, before the loop. Declaring it inside the loop resets it fresh on every single pass.

title: Lab — Process a Real List of Your Own Data
description: Take a real list from your own life — symptoms, doses, steps, spoons spent — and write a program that loops over it to produce a useful summary, not just a repeated print.

learningObjectives.text: Loop over a real list to compute a genuine summary value
Combine an accumulator with a condition to filter what gets counted
Verify a loop's result by tracing it independently of running the code

contentSections.body: A list on its own is just data sitting there. A loop is what turns it into an answer — a total, a count, an average, a "how many days this week." This lab is about building that answer from something real.

contentSections.title: Process a real list of your own data
contentSections.brief: Pick something you'd realistically track as a list of numbers: pain levels over a week, spoons spent per day, doses taken, steps per day. Write it as an array literal at the top of your program, then loop over it to compute at least one genuine summary — a total, a count meeting some condition, or both — and print a labeled result.
contentSections.deliverable: A program that reads a list you supply and produces a useful summary.

stages.title: Write your list and a plain-English question about it
stages.instructions: Write a real list of 5-8 numbers as an array literal (`let painLevels = [4, 6, 3, ...];`), based on something you'd actually track. Then write, in plain English, one specific question the list should answer — a total, an average, or a count of entries meeting some condition ("how many days was pain above 5").
stages.checkpoint: You have a real array of 5-8 numbers and one specific, answerable question written in plain English.

stages.title: Loop and build the accumulator
stages.instructions: Write a for...of loop over your list. Declare the accumulator your question needs (a running total, or a count) before the loop starts, and update it inside the loop body — using a condition inside the loop if your question involves "how many meet some criteria," the way lesson 5's counting pattern worked.
stages.checkpoint: The loop runs and the accumulator is declared outside it, updating correctly on each pass — verified by tracing at least the first two passes by hand.

stages.title: Print a labeled summary and check it by hand
stages.instructions: Print the final accumulated result with a template literal that labels what it means ("Total pain across the week: 25", not just "25"). Then, separately from running the code, add up your original list by hand (or with a calculator) and confirm the printed result actually matches — this is the self-check the architecture doc asks every lab to include.
stages.checkpoint: The printed result is labeled clearly, and you've independently verified it matches a hand calculation of the same list.

rubric.criterion: The list is real data, not placeholder numbers
rubric.meets: 5-8 values you'd actually track, tied to something real in your life.

rubric.criterion: The accumulator is declared outside the loop
rubric.meets: Initialized once before the loop starts, updated inside it — not reset on every pass.

rubric.criterion: The summary genuinely answers the stated question
rubric.meets: If the question was a count with a condition, the loop actually filters with an if, not just totals everything.
console.log prints a full sentence naming what the number means, not a bare unlabeled value.

rubric.criterion: The result was checked by hand, separately from running the code
rubric.meets: A hand calculation of the same list matches the printed output — a genuine, independent check, not just "it ran."

contentSections.body: A loop earns its place the moment it produces a real answer about real data — that's the difference between a drill and something you'd actually use.

description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from Making Decisions, two reaching back further into Variables and Types. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's core distinctions, and earlier ones, without looking them up

questions.prompt: How many times does `for (let i = 0; i < 4; i++)` run its body?
questions.explanation: i takes the values 0, 1, 2, 3 — four distinct values, four passes, stopping the moment i becomes 4.

questions.prompt: What causes a while loop to become an infinite loop?

options.label: Using while instead of for
Nothing inside the body ever changes the value the condition depends on
The starting value is too high

questions.explanation: If nothing inside the loop moves the checked value toward making the condition false, the condition stays true forever.

questions.prompt: What's the difference between break and continue?

options.label: break exits the whole loop; continue skips just the current pass and keeps looping
They do the same thing
break is for while loops, continue is for for loops

questions.explanation: break stops the loop entirely, right now. continue skips only the rest of the current pass and lets the loop carry on to the next item.

questions.prompt: Why does declaring an accumulator inside a loop's body (instead of before it) break the running total?

options.label: It doesn't — placement inside or outside the loop has no effect
It resets the accumulator to its starting value on every single pass
It makes the loop run one extra time

questions.explanation: A variable declared inside the loop body is recreated fresh on every pass, wiping out whatever it accumulated on the previous one.

questions.prompt: From Making Decisions: what's the difference between == and === in JavaScript?

options.label: == silently converts types before comparing; === requires matching type and value
They're interchangeable
=== is only for numbers

questions.explanation: == can report true for values of different types that happen to look similar (like "7" and 7). === never converts anything.

questions.prompt: From Making Decisions: what happens when a value falls through an if/else-if chain with no final else?

options.label: It throws an error
The chain silently produces no output at all
The first branch runs by default

questions.explanation: An unmatched chain with no else just produces silence — no error, no fallback — which is exactly what makes a missing case dangerous.

questions.prompt: From Making Decisions: when should you reach for && versus ||?

options.label: && when every condition must be true; || when at least one must be true
They're chosen based on which is shorter to type
&& for numbers, || for text

questions.explanation: && requires all sides true. || requires at least one side true. The wording of the rule ("both" vs "either") tells you which to use.

questions.prompt: From Making Decisions: why is > 8 different from >= 8 at the boundary value of exactly 8?

options.label: There's no real difference
>8 excludes 8 itself; >=8 includes it
>= only works with whole numbers

questions.explanation: >8 is false when the value is exactly 8, since 8 isn't strictly greater than 8. >=8 is true at exactly 8.

options.label: Form input arrives as text by default, and Number(...) converts it into a real number deliberately
It's optional — arithmetic works the same either way
It converts a number into text

options.label: Nothing — if it's valid, it's good enough
JavaScript only enforces validity (syntax rules); a good, specific name is a separate discipline the language never checks
A good name must use only single letters
